concepts.decision: Assess fit, architecture, data/identity/dependency impact, evidence, support, contract, and exit before adoption and periodically thereafter.
concepts.definition: Software or service obtained from outside the organization whose security, support, and lifecycle still affect the organization’s risk.
concepts.failureExample: A product can meet today’s feature need yet leave the organization unable to patch, audit, or exit a critical dependency.
concepts.label: Acquired Software

concepts.decision: Evaluate vendor support, update cadence, configuration, integrations, vulnerability response, and compensating controls for the intended use.
concepts.definition: Commercial off-the-shelf software supplied as a vendor product with limited customer control over source and release timing.
concepts.failureExample: Assuming a popular COTS package is secure can leave a known vulnerable configuration or unsupported version in production.
concepts.label: Cots

concepts.decision: Evaluate maintainer health, release integrity, transitive dependencies, license, internal ownership, update/review capacity, and support plan.
concepts.definition: Software whose source can be inspected and modified under its license, while maintenance, provenance, dependency, and support responsibilities remain.
concepts.failureExample: Inspectable source does not help if nobody owns timely review and updates for the deployed component.
concepts.label: Open Source

concepts.decision: Identify shared dependencies and contractually/operationally allocate notification, audit, security, resilience, and exit responsibilities.
concepts.definition: Risk arising from an external supplier’s software, service, people, subprocessors, operations, or failure to meet obligations.
concepts.failureExample: A provider incident can expose customer data when subprocessor access and notification duties were never understood.
concepts.label: Third Party Risk

concepts.decision: Use it to identify direct/transitive components, versions, owners, and update exposure; pair it with provenance, testing, and supplier evidence.
concepts.definition: A structured inventory of software components and related dependency information used to understand composition and support vulnerability response.
concepts.failureExample: An SBOM can list a component without proving the artifact was built from approved source or that the component is safe.
concepts.label: Software Bill of Materials

concepts.decision: Assess pre-contract evidence and establish ongoing monitoring, audit/notification, portability/deletion, transition, and termination terms.
concepts.definition: Risk that a vendor’s security, viability, contractual performance, updates, support, hosting, or exit behavior harms the organization.
concepts.failureExample: A vendor’s unexpected end of support can turn a patched service into an unremediable critical exposure.
concepts.label: Vendor Risk

misconceptions.claim: Open source has no supplier risk because code is public.
misconceptions.correction: Maintainer identity, dependency chain, build provenance, support, and vulnerability response still create risk.

outcome: Evaluate acquired software and services for trust, dependency, data, support, contract, and exit risks, then define controls and evidence.

sections.body: Review architecture, data flows, identities, dependencies, vulnerability history, update process, secure-development evidence, support lifecycle, licensing, privacy, hosting regions, subprocessors, resilience, incident duties, and ability to export or delete data. Use SBOM/provenance and independent evidence where available.
keyPoints: COTS and open source differ in support and control models but both carry dependency risk.
Managed service contracts must define roles and evidence.
Exit and replacement constraints are security concerns.
sections.title: Assess what enters the environment

sections.body: Use contract controls, sandboxing, least privilege, network segmentation, monitoring, patch and vulnerability commitments, compensating controls, approval gates, and periodic reassessment. Define breach notification, audit rights, portability, key ownership, deletion, transition assistance, and termination procedures before dependency becomes critical.
keyPoints: A security questionnaire is an input, not proof.
Controls must cover updates, support expiration, and subcontractors.
Exit planning reduces lock-in and availability risk.
sections.title: Manage residual and lifecycle risk

sections.body: COTS is vendor-developed software with limited customer control over source and release timing; open source provides inspectable and modifiable code but still has maintainer, dependency, license, and support risk; third-party software introduces supplier governance; managed enterprise applications shift more operation to a provider; SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS divide responsibility differently across application, platform, runtime, identity, data, and infrastructure. Assess each model for data location, tenant isolation, update authority, vulnerability disclosure, logging, subprocessor access, resilience, portability, contract rights, and secure exit.
keyPoints: More provider operation does not transfer customer data, identity, configuration, or risk accountability automatically.
Open source visibility is not the same as maintained, vulnerability-free, or supported software.
Exit requires export, deletion, key/access revocation, evidence, and continuity testing.
sections.title: Compare acquisition models and preserve exit options

learningJob.plainExplanation: Acquired software risk includes data, identities, regions, subprocessors, support, updates, incident evidence, continuity, contract rights, deletion, and exit. Vendor reputation or public source code does not replace evidence and residual-risk ownership.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: The acquisition-to-exit flow lets the learner trace data and responsibility through vendor, subprocessors, contract evidence, support, deletion, and exit.
